primitives.name: Wind Resistance Modulation
primitives.verbatim_quote: We use data from high school sprinters to explore mindset effects on 100 m finishing times and find that headwinds hamper performance more than can be attributed to the physics of wind resistance alone.
primitives.assumptions: Linear relationship between wind velocity and performance degradation; headwinds dominate over tailwinds in psychological impact.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When v_w > 2 m/s, performance deviation exceeds physical drag model predictions.

layer2.mapping: Latent belief adjustment in performance estimation due to perceived environmental stressors.
layer2.telemetry: Deviation of actual sprint times from baseline physics-derived estimates.

primitives.name: Vicarious Self-Efficacy Effect
primitives.verbatim_quote: We posit vicarious self-efficacy as a plausible explanation for these difference-in-differences patterns.
primitives.assumptions: Belief propagation via social media exposure enhances self-efficacy, leading to measurable performance gains.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Effect is significant only when E_v increases above baseline threshold and T_b is within 30 days.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to cognitive bias amplification in decision-making under uncertainty.
layer2.telemetry: Change in average sprint times pre/post Boling race, stratified by demographic groups.

primitives.name: Gendered Psychological Impact
primitives.verbatim_quote: These (implied) psychological effects of wind on sprint times are stronger for girls than for boys.
primitives.assumptions: Psychological susceptibility varies by gender due to differing belief structures and social conditioning.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Δt_g > 0.2 s for girls vs. Δt_g < 0.1 s for boys under same wind conditions.

The core insight is that belief systems—particularly vicarious self-efficacy—can modulate physical performance beyond deterministic physical laws. Wind resistance acts as a proxy for environmental stress, where psychological interpretation of such stressors leads to measurable deviations from expected performance. The Boling effect demonstrates a temporal shift in belief states that translates into quantifiable behavioral change. The heterogeneity across genders suggests that belief mechanisms are not uniform but depend on sociocultural constructs embedded in athletic identity. The Peter Pan critique is addressed by distinguishing between biophysical binding and belief-driven flexibility in non-constrained domains. The mathematical framework treats belief as a latent variable influencing outcome distributions rather than a mere scalar. This allows for probabilistic modeling of performance shifts under exogenous shocks like viral events.
